by_task.when: ARIZONA is allowable and one of those category provisions is being valued.
by_task.procedure: For each asset-exemption pair independently, use the lesser of asset value and $2,000 under § 33-1125(10), or $15,000 under § 33-1125(8). Apply § 33-1125(1) only to actual wearing apparel and § 33-1125(4) only to engagement or wedding rings. Apply § 33-1123 only to household furniture, furnishings, goods, consumer electronics, or appliances, not to jewelry merely because it is for personal use.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not treat a pendant, bracelet, or other non-ring jewelry as wearing apparel or as an engagement/wedding ring, and do not use a cap as an eligibility test. Do not place non-ring jewelry under § 33-1123 absent facts making it a listed household category.

by_task.when: FEDERAL is an allowable jurisdiction and an independently applicable § 522(d)(5) alternative must be valued.
by_task.procedure: For each asset independently, claim the lesser of its value and $1,475 plus up to $13,950 of unused § 522(d)(1) capacity. When the facts show no use of § 522(d)(1), use the full $15,425 ceiling for one debtor. Under § 522(m), apply that allowance separately to each debtor in a joint case, so the combined ceiling is $30,850. Report this alternative in addition to every matching category-specific federal alternative. Under § 522(d)(3), separately limit each particular item to the lesser of its value and $700.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not allocate the wildcard across assets, infer that another exemption consumes it, or omit it merely because a more specific exemption applies. Do not cap the wildcard at $1,475 when the supplied facts leave the residence allowance unused, report § 522(m) itself as an asset exemption, exceed the asset's value, or classify a firearm under § 522(d)(3).

by_task.when: ILLINOIS is allowable and the asset is debtor-owned personal property used personally rather than for business.
by_task.procedure: Test § 5/12-1001(b) for every such asset, including property also covered by subsection (a), (c), or (e). Claim the lesser of the asset value and $4,000 for one debtor; in a two-debtor joint case, combine the spouses' separate allowances for a ceiling of $8,000. Include this independently from applicable subsections (a), (c), or (e).
by_task.avoid_when: Do not substitute the § 5/12-1001(b) ceiling for the separate motor-vehicle cap, and do not omit the wildcard because a specific exemption also applies. Do not use these personal-property exemptions for business-use property.

by_task.when: An Oregon § 18.345(1)(p) alternative applies to personal property.
by_task.procedure: For that alternative, claim the lesser of the asset value and $400, independently of other assets and independently of any category-specific Oregon alternative. If the asset is worth less than $400, use its actual value, not $400, and retain every separately matching Oregon category provision.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit the $400 alternative because a more specific exemption applies, and do not treat its cap as authority for unrelated category exemptions. Keep § 18.345(1)(b) limited to apparel and jewelry, § 18.345(1)(d) to vehicles, and § 18.345(1)(f) to household goods, furniture and utensils.

by_task.when: An independently applicable Pennsylvania § 8123 alternative must be valued.
by_task.procedure: Claim the lesser of the asset value and $300 for one debtor. Because each spouse is entitled to the exemption, use a combined ceiling of $600 for jointly owned property in a two-debtor case. Test § 8123 for every debtor-owned property even when another Pennsylvania or federal alternative also applies.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not allocate the monetary exemption across different assets or omit it because another exemption also applies. Apply § 8124(a)(1) only to actual wearing apparel; do not invent a supplied Pennsylvania firearm or general-jewelry provision.
